lessons.title: Points per possession
lessons.objective: Explain pace, offensive rating, defensive rating and net rating.

payload.prompt: A typical NBA team completes about how many possessions per game?

explanation.correct: In recent seasons a typical NBA team has about 99 to 100 possessions a game. That count is called pace, and it shifts a little from year to year.
explanation.incorrect: An NBA team has roughly 100 possessions a game in recent seasons. Pace is that count, and it tells you how fast a team plays, not how well.

payload.prompt: An elite NBA offense scores about how many points per 100 possessions?

explanation.correct: In recent seasons the league average has been around 114 to 115, and the best offenses reach about 120. Offensive ratings drift upward over time, so always compare a team to that season's league average.
explanation.incorrect: Recent league averages sit in the mid-110s, so an elite offense is around 120. The scale has crept upward over the years, which is why comparing to the league average matters.

payload.prompt: What does an offensive rating tell you?

options.text: Points scored per 100 possessions, however fast the team plays.
The total number of points scored in a game.
How many possessions the team has per game.

explanation.correct: Offensive rating is points per 100 possessions, so it takes speed out of the picture. A fast team and a slow team can be compared fairly, because both are measured per possession.
explanation.incorrect: Total points depend on how many possessions a team gets, and possessions per game is pace. Offensive rating divides the scoring by the possessions to measure efficiency.

payload.prompt: What is net rating?

options.text: Offensive rating minus defensive rating: the margin per 100 possessions.
The team's winning percentage.
The team's average margin of victory in games it won.

explanation.correct: Net rating is what a team scores per 100 possessions minus what it allows. A positive number means it outscores opponents, and a net rating of +5 or better marks a strong team, while champions are often higher.
explanation.incorrect: Net rating is not a record or a game-by-game margin. It is the gap between offensive rating and defensive rating, and it is a better guide to team strength than wins alone.

payload.prompt: Match each metric to what it measures.

pairs.definition: How many possessions a team has per game, or per 48 minutes. It shows how fast a team plays.
Points scored per 100 possessions, which measures efficiency regardless of pace.
Points allowed per 100 possessions. Lower is better.
Offensive rating minus defensive rating, the margin per 100 possessions.

distractorDefinitions: The total number of points scored in a season.
The average score margin in games won by the team.

explanation.summary: Pace is speed; ORtg is what they score; DRtg is what they allow; NetRtg is the difference.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition of defensive rating.
payload.template: Defensive rating counts points {{what}} per 100 possessions, so a {{which}} number is better.

explanation.correct: Defensive rating is the points a team allows per 100 possessions, so fewer is better. Recent league averages are in the mid-110s, and the best defenses are well below that.
explanation.incorrect: A defense wants to allow as few points as possible, so the number counts points allowed and lower is better. The best defenses in recent seasons sit well under the league average of about 114.

lessons.title: Efficiency: eFG% and TS%
lessons.objective: Say why a three counts more in eFG% and what TS% adds.

payload.prompt: Half his shots are twos at 45%, half are threes at 35%. eFG%?

explanation.correct: Out of 100 shots he makes 22.5 twos and 17.5 threes, so his plain FG% is 40%. eFG% adds half a bucket for each three: (40 + 0.5 x 17.5) / 100, about 49%.
explanation.incorrect: eFG% is FG% with extra credit for threes: (makes + 0.5 x threes made) / shots. Here 40 makes and 17.5 threes in 100 shots gives about 49%, well above his plain 40%.

payload.prompt: He scores 25 points on 18 shots and 6 free throws. TS%?

explanation.correct: True shooting is points divided by 2 x (shots + 0.44 x free-throw attempts). Here that is 25 / (2 x 20.64), about 61%, a very good night. The 0.44 adjusts for free throws that come in pairs or trips.
explanation.incorrect: TS% = points / (2 x (FGA + 0.44 x FTA)). With 18 shots and 6 free throws the denominator is about 41.3, so 25 points is roughly 61%. That is well above the league's typical 57 to 58%.

payload.prompt: Why do teams track eFG% instead of just FG%?

options.text: A three is worth 50% more than a two, and eFG% counts that.
It includes free throws in the calculation.
It is simpler to calculate.

explanation.correct: Plain FG% treats a made two and a made three the same. eFG% fixes that by giving each made three 1.5 times the credit, so it reflects the points a shooter actually produces.
explanation.incorrect: Free throws belong to TS%, not eFG%, and eFG% is no simpler than FG%. Its point is that a made three is worth more than a made two, and FG% ignores that.

payload.prompt: A player earns lots of free throws. Which stat rewards that?

scene.alt: A player drives to the rim, absorbs contact and goes to the free-throw line several times in a game.

explanation.correct: True shooting folds free throws into the efficiency math: points divided by 2 x (shots + 0.44 x free-throw attempts). eFG% only looks at field-goal attempts, so it ignores a player who lives at the line.
explanation.incorrect: eFG% looks only at field goals, with extra credit for threes. TS% adds free throws to the picture, which is why players who draw a lot of fouls look better in it.

payload.prompt: What measures a shot's value?
payload.template: A shot's value is its {{ep}}, the average points it produces per attempt.

explanation.correct: Expected points is the make rate times the shot's value. A 35% three is worth 1.05 per shot and a 45% two only 0.90, which is why a long two is hard to justify.
explanation.incorrect: Usage rate is about possessions and pace is about speed. Expected points multiplies the make rate by the shot's value: a 35% three gives 1.05, and a 45% two gives 0.90.

lessons.title: Usage and stars
lessons.objective: Explain usage rate, PER and what a star profile looks like.

payload.prompt: What is usage rate?

options.text: The share of team possessions a player ends with a shot, free-throw trip or turnover.
How many minutes a player is on the court.
The player's shooting percentage.

explanation.correct: Usage rate is how often a player finishes his team's possessions while on the floor. With five players, 20% is the average, and high-volume stars often run 28% or more.
explanation.incorrect: Usage is about possessions, not minutes or accuracy. A player who ends a possession with a shot, a trip to the line or a turnover has used it.

payload.prompt: PER (Player Efficiency Rating) measures what?

options.text: One per-minute number that rolls up a player's box-score stats, where 15 is average.
Only the player's point total per game.
How many possessions the player starts.

explanation.correct: PER combines points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, turnovers and fouls into a single per-minute score, scaled so the league average is 15. It is popular but leans on volume scoring and undervalues defense.
explanation.incorrect: PER is not just points or possessions. It folds many box-score stats into one per-minute number, with 15 as average, and it misses a lot about defense.

payload.prompt: Complete the definition of Win Shares.
payload.template: Win Shares turn a player's stats into an estimate of team {{what}}, counting both offense and {{also}}.

explanation.correct: Win Shares divide a team's wins among its players according to what they did on both ends. A strong season for a star can be worth 10 or more, and a solid rotation player adds a few.
explanation.incorrect: Win Shares are about wins, not money or playing time. They estimate how many of a team's wins belong to each player and count offense and defense.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: His usage rate is too high for a role player.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: He is ending too many of the team's possessions for a role player.
He plays too many minutes per game.
He is fouling too much.
He is taking too few shots.

payload.translation: She thinks he is taking or losing the ball on more possessions than a role player should. The shots he takes would be better spent on the team's stars.

followUps.line: Is he actually efficient with them, though?
followUps.why: High usage is fine when a player is efficient, so it is a fair, informed question.

followUps.line: So the shots should go to the stars?
followUps.why: You are checking your read in plain words and letting her confirm it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Usage is how often a player ends a possession. About 20% is average; stars run higher. You can just ask whether he is efficient with it.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: His PER looks great, but I don't see it helping us win.

payload.question: What is she noting?

options.text: The stat says he is productive, but his play is not turning into wins.
His shooting form is bad.
He fouls too much.
He needs to play more minutes.

payload.translation: PER is a box-score efficiency number. She is saying the stat line is strong, but when she watches him, the team does not seem to benefit, so the number may be missing something.

followUps.line: What do you think the number is missing?
followUps.why: It invites her to explain, and PER is known for missing defense and fit.

followUps.line: Maybe it is a small sample?
followUps.why: It is a fair, humble check that lets her agree or disagree.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: PER is one stat, and it leans toward scoring volume. You can say 'what do you think the number is missing?' and keep the conversation going.

lessons.title: All-in-one metrics
lessons.objective: Decode BPM, VORP and the all-in-one stat family without a math degree.

payload.prompt: Match each advanced metric to what it means.

pairs.definition: An estimate from box-score stats of points per 100 possessions a player adds over an average player.
BPM turned into total value over a replacement-level player across a season.
How the team's margin per 100 possessions changes when a player is on the floor versus off.

distractorDefinitions: How many points a player scores per game.
The percentage of possessions a player handles the ball.

explanation.summary: BPM estimates impact from the box score, VORP stretches it over a season against a replacement player, and on-off simply compares the team with and without him.

payload.prompt: What does a Box Plus-Minus (BPM) of +8 mean?

options.text: He is estimated to add 8 points per 100 possessions over an average player.
He scored 8 more points than his usual average.
His team won 8 more games because of him.

explanation.correct: BPM estimates, from the box score, how many points per 100 possessions a player adds compared to an average player. A +8 would be a historically great season, since most rotation players sit near zero.
explanation.incorrect: BPM is a rate of impact per 100 possessions, not a scoring bump or a win count. +8 means an estimated 8 points per 100 possessions above an average player.

payload.prompt: Why is VORP (Value Over Replacement) useful?

options.text: It compares a player with a freely available replacement, so it shows how much he is really worth.
It ranks players by how many minutes they play.
It predicts which team will win the title.

explanation.correct: VORP asks how much better a player is than the kind of player any team could sign cheaply. Over a full season, a VORP around 2 is an All-Star-level year, and 6 or more is a clear MVP candidate.
explanation.incorrect: VORP is not a minutes ranking or a forecast. It measures a player's season value against a replacement-level player, which is useful when weighing what a contract is worth.

payload.prompt: What is the danger of relying only on all-in-one metrics like BPM or PER?

options.text: They squeeze a lot into one number and can miss things like defense and fit.
They are too complicated for anyone to understand.
They only work for players over thirty.

explanation.correct: One number can hide a lot. Box-score stats see scoring and rebounding well but catch defense, spacing and fit only partly, so the numbers work best as a starting point for a conversation.
explanation.incorrect: These metrics are useful and not age-limited. Their weakness is that one number cannot hold everything, and the box score misses much of what defenders and movers do.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Look at his on-off numbers, the team is way better with him.

payload.question: What is she showing you?

options.text: The team's scoring margin is much better with him on the floor than off it.
He plays in every game of the season.
He plays more minutes than anyone on the team.
He scores more points than anyone on the team.

payload.translation: She is comparing how the team does when he plays and when he sits. The team is clearly better with him in the game, according to on-off numbers.

followUps.line: Who is he usually on the floor with?
followUps.why: On-off numbers depend on teammates, so this is exactly the right follow-up.

followUps.line: Is it the scoring or the defense?
followUps.why: It asks her to say where the difference comes from.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: On-off is simply how the team does with a player in the game versus out. It can be noisy, so you can ask who he shares the floor with.

lessons.title: Shot charts
lessons.objective: Read a shot chart: hot zones, cold zones and the dead midrange.

payload.prompt: A shot chart shows one three at 22 feet. Tap where it is.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram with the basket near the bottom edge. The three-point line runs straight near each sideline, then curves out to the top of the arc.

explanation.correct: The corner is the only place the NBA three-point line is 22 feet from the basket. It is 23 feet 9 inches at the top, so the corner is the shortest three and a favorite shot for teams.
explanation.incorrect: Only the corner is 22 feet from the basket. The wing and the top of the arc are farther, up to 23 feet 9 inches, and a shot well behind the arc is farther still.

payload.prompt: On a shot chart, where do teams shoot best?

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram with the basket near the bottom edge. The rim area is directly under the basket, with the elbow, the midrange and the three-point line above it.

explanation.correct: Shots at the rim go in far more often than anything else, around 65% in recent seasons, so they are the most productive shot on the floor.
explanation.incorrect: Shots farther from the basket go in less often. Shots at the rim are made around 65% of the time in recent seasons, much higher than any jumper.

payload.prompt: Tap the zone that is easiest to fade: the long two.

diagram.alt: Half-court diagram with the three-point arc curving high above the free-throw line. The area between the arc and the painted lane is the midrange.

explanation.correct: The midrange is the long two. It is taken from nearly three-point distance for only two points, so its expected value per shot is lower than a three or a shot at the rim. Teams now take far fewer of them.
explanation.incorrect: The rim and the threes are the shots analytics teams want. The midrange is the zone that shot charts show teams avoiding, because it pays two points from almost three-point distance.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of a shot chart.
payload.template: A shot chart maps where each shot was {{taken}} and whether it {{result}}.

explanation.correct: A shot chart plots each attempt on a court diagram and marks makes and misses, often as a heat map of make rates by zone. It shows at a glance where a player or team is hot or cold.
explanation.incorrect: A shot chart is about shots, not plays or passes. Each attempt is placed on the court where it was taken and marked as made or missed.

payload.prompt: Why did NBA analytics kill the midrange?

options.text: The math says a long two produces fewer points per shot than a three or a shot at the rim.
Guards refused to take them.
The league banned shots from that area.

explanation.correct: A 45% long two yields 0.90 expected points per shot, and a 35% three yields 1.05. Teams followed the numbers, so the midrange is taken far less than it was. Some stars still thrive with it, which is part of the debate.
explanation.incorrect: Nothing banned the midrange and it is not about guards' feelings. Teams moved away from it because, on average, it produces fewer points per shot than a three or a shot at the rim.

lessons.title: Tracking data and play types
lessons.objective: Explain tracking data, screen assists and play-type frequencies.

payload.prompt: Complete the description of tracking data.
payload.template: Tracking data uses cameras to record where every {{what}} and the ball are, many times per {{per}}.

explanation.correct: Camera systems in every arena log each player's and the ball's position about 25 times a second. That gives analysts spacing, speed and distance data that a box score cannot show.
explanation.incorrect: Tracking data is positional: where every player and the ball are, many times each second. It is not a count of fans or whistles, and a season is far too long a unit.

payload.prompt: What is a play-type analysis?

options.text: Sorting possessions by the action that ended them, such as pick-and-roll, isolation or spot-up, and measuring how each scores.
Listing the kinds of shoes the players wear.
Counting how many fouls are called.

explanation.correct: Play-type data tags each possession, for example pick-and-roll ball handler, isolation, post-up or spot-up, and measures points per possession for each. It shows what a team relies on and what works.
explanation.incorrect: Play-type analysis is about offensive actions, not shoes or fouls. Each possession is labeled by the action that ended it, and the points per possession are tallied by type.

payload.prompt: What does a high contested-shot rate mean?

options.text: Many of his shots come with a defender close by, which means tough looks.
He gets fouled on most of his shots.
His team keeps winning close games.

explanation.correct: A shot counts as contested when a defender is within about four feet. A high rate means tough shots, and a scorer who makes them anyway is special. It can also point to poor spacing around him.
explanation.incorrect: Contested does not mean fouled or close games. It means a defender was near the shooter. The key question is how well he shoots on those looks.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He is elite at rim deterrence even though he does not get many blocks.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Opponents avoid attacking the rim when he is there, so he changes shots without many blocks.
He fouls opponents constantly.
He plays very few minutes.
He steals the ball more than anyone.

payload.translation: His presence alone scares drivers away or makes them shoot worse, even though he does not collect many blocks. Shot blocks undercount that kind of defense.

followUps.line: So blocks do not tell the whole story?
followUps.why: You are checking the idea in plain words, and she gets to say why blocks miss the point.

followUps.line: How do they measure it, then?
followUps.why: Teams measure opponents' shot frequency and accuracy at the rim when he is on the floor, and asking invites her to explain.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rim deterrence just means opponents take worse shots or fewer shots at the rim because he is there. Blocks are only the visible part.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: Too many of their possessions are isolation plays.

payload.question: What is she noting?

options.text: The team leans on one-on-one plays more than it should.
Their bench plays too many minutes.
They run too many fast breaks.
They take too many threes.

payload.translation: Play-type data breaks an offense into actions like isolation, pick-and-roll and spot-up. She thinks the team runs too many isolations, which tend to score worse than ball movement.

followUps.why: It is an honest question, and iso-heavy offenses often rely on one or two stars.

followUps.line: Does it work when it is the star?
followUps.why: Some stars are efficient in isolation, so it is a fair follow-up.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Play-type distribution is just how often a team runs each kind of action. 'Too much iso' is an opinion, and you can ask whether the stars make it work.

lessons.title: Eye test vs numbers
lessons.objective: Use stats to ask better questions instead of ending arguments.

payload.prompt: A playoff hot streak: 42% on 40 threes. Believe it?

situation.narrative: A player has made 42% of his threes in the playoffs so far, on about 40 attempts. Last season he made 34% over a full season.

options.label: Enjoy it, but expect him to settle toward 34 to 36%
options.consequence: Forty shots is a small sample, so a hot stretch like this is common even for a normal shooter. The larger sample says he is about a 34 to 36% shooter, and he will probably drift back.
considerations: 40 attempts is too few to show his true level
500+ attempts from last season is a better guide
Hot stretches are normal in small samples
Tougher playoff defense could make the gap matter more

options.label: He has clearly improved; trust the new rate
options.consequence: He might really have improved, but one series cannot prove it. If he is back at 34% next round, the hot streak was mostly noise.
considerations: Players do improve, so it is not impossible
A few weeks cannot separate skill from luck
A full season of data would tell you more

payload.expertNote: Sample size is one of the most common traps in basketball talk. A full season of shots beats one series. Stats are best used to ask whether a number is real or noise, not to end an argument.

payload.prompt: Why do analysts care about sample size?

options.text: Few shots or games can look great or awful by luck, while more of them are steadier.
Because bigger numbers are always better.
Because it decides how long the season is.

explanation.correct: Luck swings small samples a lot. A 5-for-5 night is noise, and a few hundred shots over a season says far more about a shooter. The more attempts behind a number, the more you can trust it.
explanation.incorrect: Sample size is about how much luck can move a number. Small samples swing widely, and big ones settle down, so analysts ask how many shots or games are behind a stat.

payload.prompt: What is the danger of 'clutch stats' (performance in close, late-game situations)?

options.text: A player takes only a few clutch shots a year, so luck can swing the numbers a lot.
Clutch time counts for double in the standings.
Only superstars are allowed to take clutch shots.

explanation.correct: Clutch time is usually the last five minutes of a game within five points, which is a small slice of the season. A player can look great or awful there by luck, so clutch stats are noisy year to year.
explanation.incorrect: Clutch time has no special weight in the standings and any player can take the shots. The real trap is the tiny sample: a few makes or misses swing the numbers a lot.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: His numbers were MVP-level, but I watched him get exposed on defense.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The numbers looked great, but what she saw on defense did not match.
She thinks all statistics are wrong.
She thinks he fouled out too often.
She thinks the voters ignored his offense.

payload.translation: She is saying the stat line made him look like an MVP, but watching games showed him getting beaten on defense, and box-score numbers capture that badly.

followUps.line: What did you see him get beaten on?
followUps.why: It asks her for the specific thing she noticed, which is how eye-test talk works.

followUps.line: Do the defensive numbers back that up?
followUps.why: It connects what she saw to the stats instead of pitting them against each other.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Stats and the eye test each miss things. You do not have to pick a side: ask what she saw and what the numbers say.

statement.speaker: Your crush
statement.text: He is shooting 50% from three this season.

payload.question: What is a good first question?

options.text: How many threes has he taken?
Is he a good player?
What is his free-throw percentage?
Does his team win a lot?

payload.translation: A 50% mark on 20 attempts is easy luck, and on 200 attempts it would be remarkable. Asking how many he has taken is the quickest way to tell whether the number means something.

followUps.why: It is the natural first question, and it is one nobody minds being asked.

followUps.line: Is that a career high for him?
followUps.why: It compares the number with his own history, which shows whether it is a real jump.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Asking 'how many shots is that on?' is a genuine question and a smart one. You do not need to pretend to know the answer.

payload.title: Stats vs. eye test
payload.setting: Texting after watching your crush's team play.

exchanges.theirMessage: The stats do not match what I saw in the game.

replies.text: Stats are one piece. What did you see?
replies.theirResponse: He had 20 points but was sluggish on defense.
replies.coachNote: You treated the stats and her eyes as two clues, and you got her talking. Hard to beat.

replies.theirResponse: Not really, his numbers looked fine to me.
replies.coachNote: Stats can mislead, but waving them all away ends the conversation. Both stats and eyes miss things.

replies.text: Plus-minus might show it. Want to look?
replies.theirResponse: Oh, I did not think about that.
replies.coachNote: Offering a stat to bridge the gap is nice. Plus-minus is noisy, so asking what she saw first works a little better.
